stops.narrative: Compare oral history, foreign imagery and material evidence.
Inspect the figure’s posture before naming an emotion or a ruler.
Put water, roads and farming into the urban landscape.
Explore court and scholarly purposes beside a glazed bowl.
Compare a regional production argument with the uncertainty of an object’s precise itinerary.
Separate settlement dating from the broader history of knowledge.

conclusion: Journeys, techniques, memories and infrastructures connect communities in different ways. Each needs its own evidence. A line on a map can summarize a supported connection; it cannot create one.

evidence.prompt: Which connection is described at the right level of certainty?

options.text: The tunic’s technical features support regional comparison, while its exact individual route remains unknown.
options.feedback: The catalogue makes a technical and regional argument. It does not provide a complete object itinerary.

options.text: One long date range proves an object was made both before and after a conquest.
options.feedback: A date range expresses uncertainty about when it was made, not repeated production of the same object.

options.text: A navigation tradition requires a surviving written map to count as knowledge.
options.feedback: Taonui describes memorized and practiced ways of reading stars, swells and landmarks.
